clue.text: Dreadful English summer noted by Puccini

definitions.text: Dreadful English summer noted by Puccini

parts.words: Dreadful English summer noted by Puccini
parts.note: a rotten British summer might offer just a single sunny spell, and Puccini set Butterfly's famous aria 'Un bel di' to these words

explanation.surface: A grumble about the dismal British weather, apparently set to music by an Italian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: The aria 'Un bel di vedremo' from Madama Butterfly is known in English by this title; a wet summer might manage only one sunny spell.
explanation.definitionFit: The English title of a Puccini aria, and jokingly the sole sunny spell in a washed-out British summer.

clue.text: Gas ingested by newborn child

parts.note: neon is a noble gas
ingested means ate, swallowed

explanation.surface: A baby has swallowed some gas.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical term for an infant in its first weeks of life.

clue.text: Social reformer not in bed for breakfast?

parts.note: Elizabeth Fry was the English Quaker prison reformer
someone not in bed is up

explanation.surface: A campaigning reformer, already risen, ready for the morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Fry, on the old British five-pound note, campaigned for prison reform. The question mark flags a fry-up as only one kind of breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: A plate of fried bacon, eggs and so on, a classic British morning meal.

clue.text: With recent upturn about right, one should make changes

parts.note: recent means new

indicators.note: about tells us the word for upturn goes round the abbreviation for right

parts.note: an economic upturn is a boom

explanation.surface: Someone recently on the up, reckoning they ought to shake things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts R inside BOOM to give BROOM; 'With' just joins. The proverb 'a new broom sweeps clean' describes a newcomer who makes sweeping changes.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a newcomer in charge who sweeps away old ways, as the proverb says.

clue.text: Auntie's top dog

parts.note: Auntie is a nickname for the BBC, and its chief executive holds this title

explanation.surface: An elderly relative's prize-winning pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auntie' (or 'Auntie Beeb') is a British nickname for the BBC, whose head holds this title; the surface suggests a relative's prize pooch.
explanation.definitionFit: The title held by the head of the BBC, the corporation nicknamed Auntie.

clue.text: Desires stories about the end of innocence

indicators.note: about says the word for stories goes round the letter picked next

parts.note: yarns are tales or stories

indicators.note: the end of innocence is its last letter

explanation.surface: Longings told in tales that tell of lost innocence.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are verbs for longing for something; to desire is to pine for it.

clue.text: By taking it, Greece shows determination

indicators.note: taking means the abbreviation for Greece takes the word it on after it

parts.note: GR is the international abbreviation for Greece

explanation.surface: Greece, accepting a bailout, shows resolve.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit is courage and resolve, a synonym for steadfast determination.

clue.text: Pet subject of experimental interest

definitions.meaning: a small furry rodent kept as a household pet
a person or thing used to test something out

explanation.definitionFit: Both a common rodent pet and, figuratively, anyone used as a test subject in an experiment.

clue.text: Display laziness in old Scottish county, some say

indicators.note: some say signals that the phrase is spoken and its sound gives the answer

parts.note: Ayrshire is a former county of south-west Scotland; 'in Ayrshire' said quickly gives these sounds

explanation.surface: Idleness on show somewhere in old Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayrshire is a historic Scottish county on the Firth of Clyde; 'in Ayr-shuh' run together approximates the sound. 'Display' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is sluggish reluctance to act or move, a form of laziness.

clue.text: Blue Train's first or last in Kimberley

indicators.note: the train's first letter is the one that opens the word
last in Kimberley means its final letter

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the Blue Train arrives first or last in Kimberley, South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative Party, whose members are nicknamed after it; the Blue Train is a South African luxury train.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue is the party colour of the British Conservatives, so a blue is a Conservative.

clue.text: With Blair left out we can't form this special committee

indicators.note: form tells us to rearrange the remaining letters into a new word
out says the letter for left is removed from the name

parts.note: Tony Blair, the former UK prime minister, used as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Without Tony Blair, we cannot set up this group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' drops L from BLAIR, leaving BAIR; 'form' rearranges BAIR with WECANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A small inner group of ministers formed to run a country's affairs during conflict.

clue.text: Essay about Union becoming bankrupt

indicators.note: about means the word for essay goes round the abbreviation for Union

parts.note: a paper is a written essay

explanation.surface: An essay on a trade union going broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Noun sense: a bankrupt is someone who is penniless, a destitute person.

clue.text: Cheats include a sure winner in these shows

indicators.note: include means the word for cheats has the next piece placed inside it

parts.note: cons are swindles or cheats
a cert is a racing term for a certainty, a sure winner

explanation.surface: Fraudsters rig the shows so that a dead cert wins.
explanation.walkthrough: CERT is British slang, short for certainty, for a horse that cannot lose.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical performances, which are public shows.

clue.text: Being rich, we fuss over bill — not half!

indicators.note: over places the word for fuss next to the letters before it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not half keeps only the second half of the word bill

parts.note: a to-do is a fuss or commotion

explanation.surface: Being wealthy, we make a fuss about a big invoice, not half!
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' keeps LL, the back half of BILL; 'Being' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-to-do describes the prosperous and affluent, a synonym for rich.

clue.text: Kind of hose that's a foot short

definitions.text: Kind of hose that's a foot short

parts.words: Kind of hose that's a foot short
parts.note: these knitted stockings cover the lower limb but have no foot part

explanation.surface: A garden hose that falls a foot short of the flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Hose here means stockings, not a garden pipe; these footless knitted tubes keep calves warm.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitted footless tube stockings worn by dancers, a type of hosiery missing the foot.

clue.text: Fruit and vegetable found by river

parts.note: a pea is a green vegetable

explanation.surface: Fruit and veg discovered beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A pear is a familiar orchard fruit, an example of the category.

clue.text: With bread, they kept the Roman mob happy, we're told

definitions.text: With bread, they kept the Roman mob happy, we're told

parts.words: With bread, they kept the Roman mob happy, we're told
parts.note: Juvenal said Rome's rulers placated the people with bread and public shows

explanation.surface: History tells how Roman rulers pacified the populace with food and entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman satirist Juvenal coined 'panem et circenses', bread and circuses, for the handouts and games that kept citizens quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Public spectacles in Rome's arenas, paired with free grain in Juvenal's famous phrase.

clue.text: Swing a cat, perhaps, in a game from the east

indicators.note: from the east in an across clue means read right to left, backwards

parts.note: golf is a game

explanation.surface: Swinging a cat in a game imported from the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat here is the cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip; 'perhaps' marks it as one way to beat someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog is to beat, which one might do by swinging a cat-o'-nine-tails whip.

clue.text: Chicken cooked longer gets hot inside

indicators.note: inside means the abbreviation for hot goes within the rearranged letters
cooked suggests the letters of longer are reworked

explanation.surface: A bird roasted for longer gets heated through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges LONGER into LEGORN; 'inside' puts H within it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Leghorn is a Mediterranean breed of domestic chicken.

clue.text: Enter silly song to make mischief

parts.note: to go in is to enter

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters of song are jumbled

explanation.surface: Bring in a daft song to stir up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' rearranges SONG into GSON.
explanation.definitionFit: Goings-on are dubious or improper activities, the stuff of mischief.

clue.text: Begin with a song like 12 in Hyde Park

parts.note: to open is to begin
an air is a song or tune

explanation.surface: Starting off with a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is CONCERTS; Hyde Park is a big London park famous for outdoor summer concerts.
explanation.definitionFit: Concerts held in a park are outdoor events, staged under the sky.

clue.text: Close down an annoying sort of merchant

definitions.meaning: to bring a business to an end, to liquidate it
a British slang 'merchant' who likes teasing people

explanation.definitionFit: To wind up a firm is to close it; a wind-up merchant is British slang for an incessant teaser.

clue.text: Indian city needs rain, surprisingly — it's to do with farming

parts.note: Agra is the Indian city of the Taj Mahal

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests the letters of rain end up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: An Indian city's farmers need rain, unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges RAIN into RIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Agrarian describes land, crops and agriculture, everything relating to farming.

clue.text: More relaxed form of religious justice, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means we hear the word rather than see it

parts.note: karma is the Hindu and Buddhist idea of moral cause and effect, cosmic justice

explanation.surface: A gentler version of divine retribution, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound match works in a non-rhotic British accent, where both words end in 'uh'.
explanation.definitionFit: Comparative adjective meaning more at ease, less agitated or tense.

clue.text: A helping hand, paradoxically

parts.note: a boost given by cupping hands under a climber's foot or shin; paradoxical because a hand is not a lower limb, and lower limbs go down

explanation.surface: Giving assistance that somehow contradicts itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox is that help described as a hand is named after a different part of the body, and something that points up.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for a boost or assistance, originally a hoist into the saddle.

clue.text: Mom scored nothing, unfortunately, for the Officers

indicators.note: unfortunately says the letters have come out badly, so they are rearranged

parts.note: O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Mum failed to score, sadly, for the officers' team.
explanation.definitionFit: Commodores are senior naval officers, ranking above captain.

clue.text: Bite back like a small insect

indicators.note: back says the word for bite is read in reverse

parts.note: tang is a sharp taste, bite

explanation.surface: Retaliating with a sting, just like a midge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TANG round.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnat is a tiny two-winged fly, a small insect.

clue.text: Heavy blow seen as something unique

definitions.meaning: a single hard punch that settles things
a one-off, the only one of its kind

explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially a one-punch knockout blow, and also anything one of a kind.

clue.text: East Europeans take on a role that's very different

parts.note: Poles are people from Poland in eastern Europe
an actor's part is a role

explanation.surface: Eastern Europeans taking on a contrasting role.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: as far apart as the North and South Poles, completely unlike.
